sources.content: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. Congress created it with the Federal Reserve Act, which President Woodrow Wilson signed in December 1913. A series of bank panics, especially the Panic of 1907, had convinced lawmakers that the country needed a lender of last resort. The system has 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks, including those in New York and San Francisco, overseen by a Board of Governors in Washington, D.C. The board has seven members, each appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate for a 14-year term.

Monetary policy is set by the Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC. It has 12 voting members: the seven governors, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and four of the other eleven regional bank presidents, who serve one-year rotating terms. The committee holds eight scheduled meetings a year. Its main tool is a target range for the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. Congress has given the Fed a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices.
